_why: Part 1 of the new-owner guide (first days and the systems), as data so the page is prose rather than a Python function. Quotations are in the checkable bold-quote convention, copied character-for-character from the research dossiers.

parts.title: Part 1: Your first days
parts.summary: The first night plugged in, the order to hook up water, power and sewer and to undo them, the walkaround before a trip, what to do on arrival, and the mistakes new owners make in the first week.

blocks.html: The coach has to be level before the slide-outs move and before an absorption fridge runs, the water heater has to be full before it is switched on, and the electrical load should be off while the cord goes in. Work in this order and each step makes the next one safe.

items: Park, then level. Level side to side first, then front to back. The two corrections use different tools: side to side is set with blocks or ramps under the wheels, and front to back is the small adjustment made last, with the tongue jack or the landing gear.
Chock the wheels. Chock them even on level ground, and put them in before the stabilisers rather than after.

Look at the pedestal, then test it. Test the outlet with a multimeter, or with a surge protector that has diagnostics built in, before the cord goes anywhere near it. A pedestal that is scorched, cracked or loose is one to report rather than use.

Make the power connection with the pedestal breaker off. The coach end of the cord goes in first, then the pedestal end, and the breaker goes on last. Running off a generator instead of a hookup: start the generator first, check the breaker on the generator itself, then switch the coach over to it.
Water next. Connect the drinking-water hose through a pressure regulator, then open a cold tap inside and let it run to push the air out of the lines. Do not walk away from a tank that is filling.

Fill the water heater before it is switched on. Open a hot tap and let it run until the flow is steady, with no spitting or sputtering. That is what confirms the tank is full. Only then does the electric element or the burner get switched on.
Propane last. Open the main valve slowly, and if you smell gas, stop and find out why before anything is lit.

Check the detectors. The propane and carbon-monoxide alarms run on the 12-volt system, so they should be working off the house battery from the moment you arrive, not only once the coach is plugged in.

blocks.html: Two of these steps are the ones that cause damage when they are done out of order: the cord goes in with the pedestal breaker off, and the water heater stays off until a hot tap runs without sputtering. The rest are habits rather than a strict sequence.

sections.title: Hookups: water, power, sewer, and the reverse

blocks.html: There are three hookups, and one habit covers the order of all of them: make and break each connection at the point that can arc or spill, and keep the power off while you do it. Water and power can be done in either order, whether the power comes from a pedestal or a generator. The sewer is always last to connect, because it is the one connection you do not want to disturb once it is made.

Water. The order is spigot, regulator, hose, filter, coach. One arrangement connects the regulator to the city-water inlet on the RV and hooks the hose to the regulator; another puts the regulator between the hose bib at the site and the water filter, which then connects to the hose and to the trailer. Either way the regulator sits between the park's supply and everything of yours, so it takes the pressure before the pressure reaches your plumbing.

items: Use a dedicated drinking-water hose. A garden hose is not made to carry water you drink.
Fit the pressure regulator at the spigot end.
Add an inline filter if the coach does not already have one.

Connect to the city-water inlet. The fresh-tank fill and the city-water inlet are often two separate fittings, and on some coaches a single fitting and a diverter valve do both jobs, so find out which arrangement yours has.
Turn the tap on, then open a cold tap inside and let it run to clear the air out of the lines.

blocks.html: Power. Turn off power to the RV before connecting or disconnecting the power cable. When connecting, connect the cable at the RV first and plug into the AC source second; when disconnecting, unplug from the AC source first. Turn off high-draw appliances and the coach's main breaker, make sure the pedestal breaker is off, inspect and test the pedestal, connect the coach end of a detachable cord first, connect the other end to the surge protector or pedestal, turn the pedestal breaker on, wait for the electrical management system to approve the power, then switch the coach's main breaker back on and bring appliances on one at a time. A generator feeds the same panel and the same outlets as a pedestal, so the same order applies: start it, check the breaker on the generator itself, and keep the heavy loads off while you switch the coach over.

items: Switch off the air conditioner, the water heater and other heavy loads, and switch off the coach's main breaker.
Turn the pedestal breaker off.
Inspect and test the pedestal.
If the shore cord is detachable, connect the coach end first.
Connect the pedestal end.
Turn the pedestal breaker on.
Let the surge protector or EMS run its check and approve the power.
Switch the coach's main breaker on, then bring appliances on one at a time.
Running off a generator instead of a pedestal: start the generator first and check the breaker on the generator itself, then switch the coach over to it.

blocks.html: Sewer. Connect the hose at both ends before you open anything, and keep the black valve closed. Never open the black tank valve and leave it open throughout your stay. Dump the black tank when it is at least two-thirds full, then the gray tank. Dumping the black tank first and the gray second lets the gray water rinse the hose.

items: Wear gloves. Fit a clear elbow at the outlet so you can see what is moving: it is the only window into the black tank.
At a dump station with a smooth inlet, a rubber donut, sometimes called a sewer doughnut or hose adapter, makes the hose fit snugly against the station inlet. Some campgrounds require one.
Open the gray valve for a short burst and close it again, so that any leak shows up as gray water rather than black. Better to find a leak with gray water than with black tank fluid.
Weight the elbow with a rock or a brick so the hose cannot kick loose. Most dump stations have a rock nearby for exactly this purpose.
Dump black, then gray, then close both valves.
Precharge the empty tank so it does not start dry. After dumping, add 5 to 10 gallons of water and treatment chemical before using it again.

blocks.html: Disconnect, in reverse. Switch the loads off, turn off the breakers, unplug from the pedestal, then disconnect the coach end of the cord. In shorthand: power off first, pedestal end first, coach end second. The same holds for every shore power connector: the pedestal breaker goes off before anything is plugged in or unplugged. A generator gets the same treatment: shut it down, or switch the coach off it, before the cord is plugged or unplugged.

The single most expensive habit in the first week is leaving the black tank valve open at a full-hookup site. The liquid runs away and the solids stay behind, and the tank slowly builds a pile that no amount of flushing removes. Keep the valve closed until the tank is at least two-thirds full.

A walkaround is a fixed loop around the coach before every departure, done in the same direction each time so that nothing is skipped. The point is not a detailed inspection. It is to catch the handful of things that are dangerous or expensive when they are left loose or left behind.

items: Tires. Check pressure against the figure on the coach's placard, not the number on the sidewall, and look for cuts and bulges. Two age facts matter. The build date is the last four digits of the DOT code: the first two digits are the week from 01 to 52, and the last two are the year. A tire can be too old while still looking new, so replace a tire that has been in service six years or more even if it looks serviceable and has not reached the treadwear limit. Check tread depth with a coin: a tire is unsafe when the minimum tread depth reaches 2/32 inch, the distance between the top of Lincoln's head and the edge on a penny.

Height. Know the tallest point of the coach before you drive anywhere, because an awning, an antenna and an air conditioner all add to it. Measure from the ground all the way to the top of the highest object on the RV, then post that number on your dashboard so you do not forget it.

The hitch or the coupling. For a trailer, the tongue weight wants to be roughly a tenth to a sixth of the loaded trailer weight, which is 10 to 15 percent. Load the heavy items low and forward, and keep them out of the back. Never load heavy items in the back of the trailer or on the back bumper.

Everything that folds, slides or latches. Awning in, antenna down, steps up, slide-outs in, roof vents closed, compartment doors latched. Use a checklist every time you arrive at or leave a campsite, because it is easy to forget simple things like unplugging power cords or lowering the TV antenna.
Propane while moving. Turn the propane supply off at the tank while driving.

blocks.html: A checklist is not a sign of inexperience. The failures it prevents are the familiar ones: an awning left out, a television antenna left up, or a cord still plugged in as the coach pulls away.
Arrival is a sequence too, and the first step happens before you drive onto the site.

items: Check in, then look at the site on foot. Walk the pad before you commit the coach to it, and note which side the pedestal and the sewer connection are on, so you park with the connections within reach.
Do not cut across your neighbour. Do not cut through another occupied site to reach the bathroom, the lake, or a trail.
Back or pull in with a spotter. Use someone outside who can see what you cannot, and agree on the hand signals before you start.
Level, then chock. Side to side first, then front to back, as set out above.
Hook up water, power and sewer in the order given earlier, keeping the black valve closed.

Keep the noise reasonable. If you can hear it two sites away, it is too loud. Official quiet hours might end at 8 AM, but generators and slide motors before 8 AM are rude even if they are technically permitted.

blocks.html: Some rules apply before you leave home. How long an RV can be parked in a residential driveway varies by municipality and HOA, so it is worth a quick check of your local ordinance.

sections.title: The mistakes people make in the first week

blocks.html: The first-week mistakes are remarkably consistent, and most of them are planning mistakes rather than operating mistakes. The machines can be learned in an afternoon. A rushed plan cannot be fixed at the campsite.

items: Going too far on the first day. Most experienced RVers prefer traveling between 200 and 330 miles per day. A new owner who plans a long first day arrives tired, in the dark, at a site they have never seen.
Skipping the shakedown trip. Take a short, close-to-home shakedown trip before venturing off on a longer one. A first trip that is also the first use of everything is a first trip with no margin.

Making the first trip hard. Book somewhere forgiving, a full-hookup park with pull-through sites rather than a tight loop. Pick a destination within one to three hours from home and stay two or three nights.
Not capturing the walkthrough. The dealer handover is the one time someone who knows the coach shows you how it works. Record the orientation so you can refer to it later.
Overpacking. Every RV has weight limits, and staying under them is vital to a smooth trip.
Taking delivery with known faults. Before you sign, the problems belong to the dealer. If your inspection finds significant issues, refuse to take delivery until they are resolved.

Missing the warranty window. After 90 days, these items are no longer covered. The 90-day provision usually covers the small adjustment items a first season shakes loose, so write the list down as you find things rather than remembering at the end.
Leaving the black valve open at a full-hookup site, which is covered above and belongs on this list anyway.

parts.title: Part 2: The systems
parts.summary: How the 12-volt and 120-volt systems divide the work, how shore power is tested and sized, how water and propane behave, what each appliance needs, and what is settled and what is not on slide-outs, leveling and electronics.

sections.title: The two electrical systems, and the rule for each

blocks.html: An RV carries two electrical systems at once, and almost every beginner confusion comes from that one fact. Every RV has two separate electrical systems: a 12-volt DC system and a 120-volt AC system. The 12-volt system is powered by the RV's battery bank and runs things like lights, water pumps, exhaust fans, and control boards for appliances. The 120-volt system powers heavier appliances and outlets, similar to a home, and comes from shore power, a generator, or an inverter. This is what runs air conditioners, microwaves, and standard plug-in devices.

head: System
Powered by
Typical loads
rows: The house battery, kept charged by the converter
Lights, water pump, furnace blower and controls, vent fans, slide and jack motors, fridge control boards, propane and carbon-monoxide detectors, thermostats
Shore power, a generator, or an inverter
Air conditioning, microwave, the electric water-heater element, household outlets, a household-style television

blocks.html: The distinction to hold onto is about when each one works. The 12-volt system works all the time as long as the batteries have charge. The 120-volt system only works when you are plugged into shore power, running a generator, or using an inverter. A furnace is the clearest example of an appliance that uses both: the burner runs on propane, but the fan that moves the heat runs on 12 volts, so a furnace will not work off a flat battery even with a full propane tank.

Converter, inverter, battery. The four words that confuse new owners are easier once the direction of travel is clear. A converter goes from AC to DC; an inverter goes from DC to AC; an inverter/charger does both; the battery stores DC. A converter converts 120-volt AC to 12-volt DC to power low-voltage DC loads, charges the battery, and distributes both 12-volt and 120-volt current to the various branch circuits in the RV. Almost every RV has a converter. Inverters are optional and are most often factory fitted on coaches with residential refrigerators or off-grid packages. A quick way to tell the two faults apart: flat batteries while plugged in is converter territory, while dead outlets while boondocking is inverter territory. An inverter only feeds the outlets wired to it, and circuits that are generally not included in inverter loads are air conditioners, refrigerators, washer-dryers, and other high-current-draw loads.

The rule: if a load plugs into a wall outlet, or is a heavy appliance such as an air conditioner, a microwave or a water-heater element, it is 120 volts AC and works only with shore power, a generator or an inverter. If a load is a light, a pump, a fan or a control board, it is 12 volts DC and works whenever the house battery has charge.

When something stops working, check it in a fixed order: name the failed load, identify whether it needs AC, DC or both, confirm the source, check the protection, and inspect the wiring and the device last.

Battery sizing is the one electrical question with no published universal answer. The amp-hour capacity a coach needs depends on its loads and how it is used, and no manufacturer gives a formula. The sizing calculators that circulate are practitioner tools rather than specifications, so they can guide a choice but cannot settle one.

An RV is not wired like a house, and the difference is a safety rule rather than a curiosity. In an RV the neutral and ground conductors are isolated; in a house they are bonded together at the service panel. Never connect neutral to ground, because that creates a ground fault, and a ground fault means shock and fire risk. More than one source can be live at once. A coach may be energised by shore power, the generator, an inverter and the batteries at the same time, so verify every source before you touch any wiring. De-energise before you open anything. Disconnect the shore cord, shut the generator down, and switch the inverter off before going near the 120-volt breaker box or any of the 120-volt wiring. To work out what any one appliance draws on either system, the watts to amps calculator does the arithmetic.

sections.title: Shore power: the pedestal, 30 amps and 50 amps

blocks.html: The pedestal is the post at the campsite that carries the receptacles and, usually, the breakers. It carries some combination of a household-style outlet, a 30-amp RV outlet and a 50-amp RV outlet, and which ones are present varies by park and by the age of the site. Or a generator, which does the same job. A generator makes its own 120 volts and feeds the same panel and the same outlets the pedestal would. Two things change: you have to start it, and you have to check the breaker on the generator itself. Everything below about loads, breakers and protection applies to a generator exactly as it does to a pedestal.

head: Service
Voltage
Connector
Maximum power
rows: Well below the 30-amp figure; use it for charging and small loads only
120 V, or 240 V on a large one
Set by the generator: a small one is around 2,000 to 4,000 watts

blocks.html: The arithmetic is why the two services are not close. A 30-amp shore cord is rated at 120 volts, so the most it can deliver is 3,600 watts. A 50-amp cord is rated at 240 volts, so the most it can deliver is 12,000 watts. A 50-amp supply therefore carries close to three times the power of a 30-amp one.

Test it before the cord goes in. The pedestal breaker goes off first, then the outlet is tested with a multimeter or with a surge protector that has diagnostics built in. Three green indicator lights is a pass. On a fail, do not connect: move the coach to another pedestal, or have the fault corrected. A pedestal that is scorched, cracked or loose is one to report rather than use.

items: Turn off high-draw appliances and the coach's main breaker.
Turn the pedestal breaker off.
Inspect and test the pedestal.
Connect the coach end of the cord first, then the pedestal end.
Turn the pedestal breaker on.
Let the EMS approve the power, then switch the coach's main breaker on and bring appliances on gradually.

blocks.html: Adapters: stepping down is normal, combining is not. A dogbone adapter changes the shape of a plug; it does not create power. Running a 30-amp coach on a 50-amp pedestal, or a 50-amp coach on a 30-amp pedestal, is routine. In the second case you are limited to 3,600 watts and will probably trip breakers if you run several heavy appliances at once, because the pedestal's 30-amp breaker is now the smallest thing protecting you.

A cheater box is the one that is not safe. A cheater box or Y-adapter combines two smaller outlets to feed a 50-amp inlet, and it is not approved for RV use. The 20-amp outlet on a pedestal has to carry GFCI protection, so the cheater trips that breaker and leaves you on the 30-amp side only. The worse case is miswiring: if one of the 30-amp receptacles is wired with reverse hot and neutral, plugging in a Y-adapter makes a hot-to-neutral short, and the arc flash can melt the contacts and injure your eyes. The 30-plus-20 version is not a workaround.

Do not chain a step down and back up. Going from a 50-amp outlet down to a 30-amp extension cord and back up to a 50-amp inlet removes the protection: nothing stops you drawing more than 30 amps, and the pedestal will supply it. A 15-amp cord in that chain is worse, because 30 amps through it reaches the boiling point of water in about five minutes. Match the adapter to the difference in plug shape, and size the protection device to the coach's own shore cord, not to the pedestal.

Surge protector or EMS: these are not the same device. A basic surge protector absorbs power spikes and does nothing else. It does not check wiring faults, voltage or ground. An EMS monitors voltage continuously, protects against surges and spikes, and detects open ground, open neutral and reverse polarity. When it finds a problem it disconnects the coach before damage happens. The thresholds most units publish are a cut-out below 102 volts or above 132 volts, with power restored automatically once the voltage settles.

The fault most likely to cost you money is not lightning. Sustained low voltage is. It makes motors draw more current, and it destroys air conditioner compressors, so a device that disconnects on low voltage is worth more than a plain surge protector. One device, sized to the coach, is enough: a 50-amp coach takes a 50-amp protector and a 30-amp coach takes a 30-amp one, with dogbone adapters to cover whatever the pedestal offers.

The hazards behind the device. On a 50-amp supply a broken neutral is the worst case, because the two 120-volt legs stop sharing the load evenly. One leg can see 80 volts while the other sees 160, and anything connected to the high leg can be destroyed almost instantly. Reverse polarity is more forgiving than it is usually described: modern appliances have isolation transformers and double insulation, and a coach's neutral and ground should be separated at the panel. It is still worth reporting, because a pedestal wired backwards was never tested after it was installed, and there is no telling what else is wrong with it.

One hazard no consumer device detects. A reverse polarity bootleg ground is not discoverable by a standard meter test, a three-light outlet tester, or the most expensive EMS units on the market. Whether current protection units have closed that gap is not established.

Where the numbers get soft: the 80 percent rule. The usual guidance is to keep a continuous draw under 80 percent of the breaker, which on a 30-amp circuit means about 24 amps. That figure comes from experienced owners rather than from a manufacturer or the electrical code, so treat it as good practice rather than a published limit.

Water enters an RV in two different ways, and they do different jobs. A freshwater connection adds potable, safe to drink, water to fill the RV's freshwater tank. Most freshwater connections are gravity fill, meaning there is an opening in the side of the RV for filling the tank with fresh water. The other way is the city-water connection, which pressurizes the coach's plumbing directly from a tap. In many and even most RVs, the fresh-water and city-water connections are separate, so there are two connections. Some coaches use a single inlet and a diverter valve, so a new owner has to find out which arrangement the coach has before the first hookup.

items: Tank and pump. Off the tank, a demand pump pressurises the system. When you are not hooked up to city water, the 12-volt fresh-water pump pressurizes the system from the onboard tank, typically outputting 1 to 4 gallons per minute at 35 to 55 PSI.

City water. On a city-water connection the park's pressure does the work, and the pump should be off. On a combined system, city-water mode supplies water from the city-water connection to your fixtures, bypassing the freshwater tank, so the pump is not needed; tank mode lets you pump water from the freshwater tank to your fixtures.

blocks.html: The pressure regulator is not optional. When connected to any pressurized water source, such as a city-water connection at a campground, using a water pressure regulator is essential. RV manufacturers generally recommend that the pressure supplied to an RV not exceed 60 psi, with a comfortable recommended pressure of around 40 to 50 psi, and the regulator itself is usually designed to hold pressure between 40 and 50 psi. Always use a pressure regulator when connecting to city water, especially when traveling or camping, because the pressure at some campgrounds can be significantly higher than recommended. Standard RV plumbing is designed to operate between 40 and 60 PSI, so a regulator is an absolute must-carry.

items: Fit the regulator at the spigot.
Then the drinking-water hose.
Then the inline filter, if the coach does not already have one. Many owners wisely add an inline water filter if their RV is not already equipped with a built-in whole-house filter.
Then the city-water inlet on the coach.

blocks.html: Do not run the pump on city water. The two systems are meant to be used one at a time. If a coach is hooked to city water with the pump accidentally left on, and a check valve has failed while park pressure is low, the pump can push its entire fresh tank back into the park's supply. The pump's job and the city connection's job overlap, and running both is how a tank empties itself overnight. Connect to city water and make sure the water pump is turned off. The corollary matters off-grid too: running the pump dry will burn it out.

Propane runs the absorption fridge, the water heater, the furnace and the range. The system itself is simple: a tank, a regulator, a main valve, and appliances with their own burner valves. The rule that matters most is the one for a leak, and it is worth knowing before the first tank is opened.

items: Put out any flame, and do not operate a switch, a light, an appliance or a phone that could spark.
Get everyone out of the RV immediately.
Shut the gas off at the tank only if you can do it safely.
Leave the area and call for help.

blocks.html: The reason to smell low is a property of the gas: propane vapor is heavier than air and may collect initially at floor levels, so a check of the coach means checking the low spots first. When the supply goes back on, open the main valve slowly, which lets the tank's excess-flow device settle rather than trip. While the coach is moving, turn the propane supply off at the tank.
A propane flame should burn blue. A yellow flame means the burner is not getting the air it needs, and that is a service item rather than something to live with.

sections.title: The appliances: fridge, water heater, furnace, air conditioning

blocks.html: The absorption fridge, and why level matters. Most RV fridges of this kind cool by a gravity-fed process with no compressor, which is why the coach has to be level for one to work well. Because the absorption system uses no mechanical pumps or compressors to circulate the refrigerant, proper leveling is required to keep the refrigerant flowing in the gravity-feed system. Without proper leveling, refrigerant collects and stagnates in the cooling coils and the cooling process stops. The practical requirement is that the vehicle be leveled so it is comfortable to live in, with no noticeable sloping of the floor or walls, and any time the vehicle is parked for several hours with the refrigerator running it should be leveled to allow proper cooling. The fridge can run on two energy sources: an automatic energy selector control system chooses between 120 volts and propane. At altitude, use the electric source: always operate the refrigerator on electric power at altitudes higher than 5,500 feet. A compressor fridge is different: it does not care about level.

The fridge's tilt limit has no published number from the maker, only the requirement that the coach be level enough to live in with no noticeable sloping of the floor or walls. The widely repeated figures of three degrees side to side and six front to back appear only in secondary sources and are attributed inconsistently, so they are not a manufacturer specification. Treat 'no noticeable slope' as the requirement.

The water heater: fill it before you switch it on. This is the most expensive mistake in the appliance section, because the electric element burns out in seconds when it is dry. The tank must be filled with water before the water heater is operated: operating it without water can damage the tank or the controls, and that damage is not covered by the limited warranty. To fill and confirm it, fill the tank with water, open both the hot and cold faucets to expel air from the tank, and when water flows from the faucets, close both and check every connection for leaks. The electric side is the fragile one, because elements can burn out quickly when they are switched on with an empty tank. On gas there is no pilot light to light by hand: the appliance has an ignition device that lights the burner automatically, so do not try to light it by hand. On a first start after the gas lines have been open, the water heater may need several ignition cycles before all the air is purged.

Check the brand before you buy or fit an anode rod. Suburban steel tanks use one, and it wants replacing about yearly. Atwood and Dometic aluminum tanks do not use one at all, and fitting one can damage the tank. In Dometic's own words: "Dometic & Atwood Brand Water Heaters DO NOT use Anode Rods!" This brand split is the most useful single thing to know about RV water heaters.

The furnace. A furnace is a good example of an appliance that uses two systems at once: the heater runs on propane, but the fan that blows hot air through the RV runs on the coach batteries, so the furnace uses both the propane and battery systems. To start it, open the LP gas tank valve by turning it fully counter-clockwise, then set the thermostat. The furnace fan should start to blow immediately after the thermostat is set, and the burner lights about 30 seconds later. A furnace with a low battery will often not light at all, because the blower has to spin before the burner will.

Air conditioning. Air conditioning is a 120-volt load, so it needs shore power, a generator or a large inverter. Its one peculiarity is the restart delay: trying to restart the air conditioner compressor before the pressure equalizes is known as short-cycling, and some but not all RV air conditioner thermostats have built-in time delays to prevent it. A generator has to be sized for the surge of a compressor starting, not just its running draw.

head: Appliance
Runs on
Needs
rows: Propane or 120 V, plus 12 V for its control board
A level coach for the absorption type
A full tank of water before either source
Charge in the house battery to spin the blower
Shore power, a generator, or a large inverter

sections.title: Slide-outs, and when to extend them

blocks.html: A slide-out runs on 12-volt motors, so it wants a healthy battery or another source of 12-volt power while it moves. On a motorhome that usually means the engine running: the ignition key must be in the on or run position to operate the slideout rooms, and the park brake must be applied for the rooms to run. Keep the engine running while extending or retracting the slideout rooms so the engine alternator can provide maximum power for proper operation of the slideout mechanisms. Ample voltage can also come from attaching the RV to shore power or turning on the generator. On a trailer there is no engine, so the slide runs off the house battery, or off the tow vehicle through the 7-way cord if the battery is low.

Extend and retract the room all the way, never part way, because a slide-out must be fully open or closed to maintain its seal and keep the interior waterproof. Keep people and objects clear of the inside and outside of the slideout room when operating: "Failure to comply could result in death or serious injury." And never drive with a room extended.

Where sources conflict: level first or slide first. Winnebago's manual for a motorhome says to level the coach and then extend the slide. Lippert's hydraulic fifth-wheel guidance says the unit must be leveled before the slideouts move: "Unit must be leveled prior to extending the slideouts to ensure coach will not move during operation of Slideout System and to provide the unit with a firm foundation." Other makers have reportedly reversed their own published order between model years. There is no universal rule, so the only defensible instruction is to follow the manual for your own make and model.

Two smaller habits are worth knowing. A Schwintek-style slide wants the switch held after the room stops: hold the switch for 5 seconds once the room is fully open or closed so the control board can complete its calculations, or the room will go out of synchronization over time. And the outside corner of a slide sits at head height on many coaches, which is why owners fit a slit foam noodle over it: the corners can be sharp and pointy, and a lack of attention could put someone into one. Remove the noodle before you close the slides.

sections.title: Leveling and stabilising are not the same job

blocks.html: Leveling corrects the slope the coach is parked on. Stabilising reduces the rocking that people and movement cause. The two are done by different hardware, and the most common warning is not to confuse them: while levelers can technically stabilize, stabilizers cannot level. The distinction matters because using stabilizers for leveling can result in ineffective performance and potential damage to your RV.

The two parts do different jobs. Leveling jacks are designed to support the weight of the RV and adjust its position as needed, while stabilizers, also known as stabilizer jacks, are not intended for leveling purposes. Stabilizers are designed solely for enhancing stability and should not be used for leveling.

items: Position the trailer, then level side to side with blocks or ramps under the wheels.

Level front to back with the tongue jack or the landing gear: place the trailer in the designated position, use leveling blocks or ramps to reach the desired level before stabilizing, then deploy the stabilizers or scissor jacks once the RV is leveled.
Chock the wheels.
Lower the stabilisers last, to contact only. If the RV begins lifting when the jack is applied, too much pressure is being used.

blocks.html: A stabiliser that lifts the coach is doing a job it was not made for. If the stabilizer manual says contact only, stop when the foot is planted and the slack is removed. Chocks are separate again and are used whatever the ground is like: install the wheel chocks first and the wheel stabilizers second. And a leveler is never a parking brake, because levelers are not designed for any type of vehicle braking.

The reasons to level: the absorption fridge is the best-supported one, and comfort is the other. The claims that a tilted coach drains its tanks badly or twists its frame are widely repeated but are not established.

sections.title: Entertainment and electronics: the reality check

blocks.html: The television is the easy part. Most RV televisions are a 120-volt load, so they work on shore power or a generator, and over-the-air reception comes from an amplified antenna on the roof. The harder part is connectivity, and this is the area with the most marketing and the least honesty, so the useful material is the material that argues against buying something.

A cellular booster does one thing: it amplifies a signal that already exists. It cannot create one. Boosters are often promoted online as a game changer that every RV and boat should have onboard, but in many situations they might not make any difference to your internet performance, and they can sometimes make data slower. The technical reason is that a booster uses a single exterior antenna: it cannot take advantage of MIMO, because it can only work with a single signal at a time. It is the equivalent of plugging one of your ears: you can still hear, but not as well. Testing has found that MIMO antennas are the optimal signal-enhancing choice for data more than 80 to 90 percent of the time.

items: A booster helps with distance to the tower, with obstacles, and with a metal-bodied coach. It does not help when there is no signal, when the tower is congested, or when you are being throttled.
It boosts cellular frequencies only. It cannot help with getting a better Wi-Fi signal.

The bands a legal consumer booster may use are limited: the bands legally approved for mobile consumer boosters include Bands 2, 4, 5, 12, 13, and 25, but many cellular carriers use and depend on several bands that are not on this list. Some boosters sold online boost bands that are not permitted, and using them can result in a knock on your door by the FCC.
Placement does as much work as the device: exterior pickup, interior router location, and cable runs can make or break real-world Wi-Fi performance.

blocks.html: The three tools people call a booster are not the same tool. RV WiFi booster is a broad, often imprecise term: depending on the product, it may mean a cellular signal booster, an RV WiFi extender, or a router that creates WiFi inside the RV from a cellular connection. These are different tools, and choosing the wrong one will not solve the connectivity problem you actually have. Start by deciding whether the problem is weak cellular or weak campground Wi-Fi, because the two need different gear. And distrust the headline numbers: marketing materials often cite up to 50 dB gain, or coverage of 5,000 square feet, or working with all carriers, but these are laboratory or ideal-case numbers.
